title: Artemis Fowl Animated Series Greenlit for Disney Channel & Disney+, Author Eoin Colfer Serves as EP at NYCC—Deadline
body:
The beloved Irish author Eoin Colfer has confirmed that Disney will bring his cult‑favorite series Artemis Fowl to the small screen as an animated show, slated to air on both Disney Channel and the Disney+ streaming platform. The announcement, made during a packed panel at New York Comic‑Con, marks the first official adaptation of the twelve‑book saga since the franchise’s debut in 2001 and positions the project as a flagship offering for Disney’s expanding family‑friendly slate.

Colfer, who will serve as an executive producer on the series, revealed that Disney’s animation studios have been developing the concept for several years, working closely with the author to preserve the tone and wit that made the books a global phenomenon. “We’re building a world that feels both magical and grounded, just as the novels did,” Colfer said, emphasizing his involvement in script development and character design. The series will reportedly follow the teenage criminal mastermind Artemis Fowl II as he navigates a covert war between the human world and an underground society of technologically advanced fairies, leprechauns, and other mythic beings.

The move comes at a time when Disney is aggressively expanding its animated portfolio, leveraging nostalgic properties to attract both legacy fans and a new generation of viewers. The decision to launch the show simultaneously on Disney Channel and Disney+ reflects a broader industry trend of “dual‑window” releases that aim to maximize reach across linear and streaming audiences. Analysts predict that the series could become a key driver of subscriber growth for Disney+, especially among families seeking content that balances clever humor with high‑stakes adventure.

Industry insiders note that the Artemis Fowl adaptation arrives after a series of mixed results for live‑action reboots of beloved books, such as the recent Disney‑produced film that failed to recoup its budget. By opting for animation, Disney sidesteps the pitfalls of casting and visual effects that often plague live‑action versions, while retaining the flexibility to depict the series’ intricate fantastical technology and fairy realms. Moreover, the animated format allows for a serialized narrative structure, giving writers the latitude to explore subplots and character arcs that were compressed or omitted in the original novels.

Fans of the books have expressed cautious optimism, citing the author’s direct involvement as a reassuring sign that the adaptation will stay true to the source material. Social media buzz indicates that long‑time readers are eager to see iconic scenes—such as the high‑speed hovercraft chase over the Irish countryside—reimagined with modern animation techniques. At the same time, newcomers to the franchise may be drawn in by Disney’s reputation for high‑quality family entertainment, potentially revitalizing interest in the printed series and associated merchandise.

Looking ahead, the production team has hinted at a multi‑season rollout, with each season covering roughly two books from the original series. If the initial episodes resonate with audiences, Disney could also explore spin‑offs focusing on supporting characters like the tech‑savvy fairy Holly Short or the enigmatic dwarf Butler. As the first episodes near completion, the entertainment world will be watching to see whether Artemis Fowl can successfully transition from page to screen and become a cornerstone of Disney’s next wave of animated storytelling.
